hypotheses.root_cause: Not determined from the logs. The best-supported lead is that the MMIO target (or its slave port) never answered DMA transaction 0xB6BA, while the fabric was nearly idle. That is not a fabric-wide deadlock, a DMA burst overflow or a power/clock event. The QoS starvation seen earlier (CPU0, 3201 ms) is a weaker alternative: it hit a different initiator and had cleared 726 ms before the timeout.
hypotheses.rationale:
Causal chain: Congestion burst at 3153-3531 ms in the CPU<->PCIE and PCIE<->DDR regions, with CPU0 QoS credit starvation at 3201 ms -> congestion clears (txn_q low/med, stall_pct 2-11 from 3560 ms) -> DMA issues txn 0xB6BA to MMIO -> MMIO target/port never responds (suspected; not confirmed) -> NOC timeout rc=-62 (ETIME) at 3927 ms -> NOC0 register snapshot at 3978 ms -> SYSTEM FATAL interconnect failure at 3995 ms. All four specialists agree on what is missing.
- NOC logs have none of the catalogued deadlock or burst markers: no 'Dependency cycle suspected', no 'DMA burst overflow', no burst_len line. The two most similar past runs (000021, 000010) both had these markers.
- PMU shows no droop, power gating, clock gating or DVFS event around the timeout.
- FW kept ticking 47 ms after the timeout and logged no WARN or ERROR at any point in the run.
- BOOT shows no late re-init or reset.
- The only catalogued marker in the run is QoS starvation, and it doesn't fit: it was CPU0, not DMA, it hit different regions (not DMA->MMIO), and it was over long before the timeout. At the moment of the timeout the fabric was nearly idle (txn_q=low, stall_pct=2). That points to a target-side non-response rather than congestion inside the fabric.
- The deciding evidence is the NOC0 register snapshot, which nobody can decode without its field map. One more question to a specialist won't settle this; it needs the register map and target-side visibility. So I'm submitting OTHER with low confidence, and RC_NOC_QOS_STARVATION is the fallback if the decoded registers show the DMA port out of credits. (0 of 4 specialists pointed at this cause.)
recommended_actions: Decode the 20-word NOC0 snapshot (0x60000A86-0x60000AD2) using the NOC0 register map: find the timed-out port, outstanding transaction counts, per-port credit counters (especially the DMA initiator's QoS credits) and which router stalled first.

Find the MMIO target that txn 0xB6BA (dst=MMIO) was addressed to and check whether it was alive: read its status/clock/reset registers after the failure and check its slave-port response logic for a missing or dropped completion.
Turn on DMA descriptor/burst logging in FW (burst size, queue depth, target address, retries) and rerun, to rule DMA burst overflow in or out directly.

Rerun with the CPU<->PCIE/PCIE<->DDR congestion workload removed, or with the QoS weights changed. If the timeout persists, QoS starvation is ruled out; if it disappears, revisit the QoS-starvation hypothesis.
Add BOOT init-completion milestones for MMIO target init and NOC0 routing/QoS setup, so incomplete initialization can be ruled out in later runs.

trace.note: This is a NOC_TIMEOUT on a DMA->MMIO transaction, followed by a fatal interconnect error. The two closest past incidents were also NOC timeouts: one a NoC deadlock (sim 0.907) and one a DMA burst overflow (sim 0.866). So NOC goes first to decode the register dump and tell those two apart. FW is next because it sets up the DMA bursts, which covers the overflow case. PMU is there to check whether the MMIO target was power- or clock-gated, a common upstream cause of unanswered transactions. BOOT was the second most active subsystem, so it may point to unfinished init or reset of the target or fabric. DDR, PCIE and THERMAL are not part of the DMA->MMIO path and didn't stand out, so they are left out.
